summary.one_liner: A short, didactic Go project that builds a simple video encoder from scratch, going from raw RGB24 frames to YUV420P, then run-length encoding and DEFLATE compression.
summary.what_it_does: The repository walks through a basic video encoding pipeline in a single main.go file, which the README says is about 120 lines of code. You feed it a raw RGB24 video file through stdin (for example, cat video.rgb24 | go run main.go). The program converts the frames to YUV420P, which halves the size by subsampling chroma. It then applies run-length encoding (RLE) and DEFLATE compression, logging the size and percentage of the original after each stage. The README's sample run shows the output going from about 54 MB raw to about 5.5 MB with DEFLATE, roughly 10% of the original. The README describes this as a teaching exercise rather than a full codec and mentions that more modern codec features could be added if there is interest. It also includes a sample video credited to Ketut Subiyanto, and a "Other languages" section that lists a Rust link.
use_cases: experimenting with run-length encoding on video data
comparing RLE and DEFLATE compression ratios on raw video
how_to_run: Open main.go to read the encoder code
notable: Implemented in about 120 lines of Go, meant to be read as a tutorial
Reports size after each stage: raw, YUV420P, RLE, and DEFLATE
Reads raw RGB24 video from stdin, with no container or file-format parsing described
Sample output shows DEFLATE reducing the raw data to about 10% of its original size
caveats: Explicitly a didactic exercise, not a comprehensive or production codec
Uses no inter-frame prediction or other modern codec features, according to the README
Requires a raw video.rgb24 input file, which the README does not provide
